Limited-edition drop: stock reservation design (design doc)

The shop has 4 units of a limited-edition item in stock, and 5 customers (c1, c2, c3, c4, c5) try to buy
it at the same time. Each customer's checkout runs on its own server thread; the threads interleave
arbitrarily. A checkout first reserves a unit (a hold), then the customer pays to confirm the
purchase.

Holds are temporary: a hold that is not paid for expires after 4 clock ticks, and the unit goes
back into stock so that another customer can buy it. Customers can be slow to pay; the payment step
may happen at any later time.

Reserving. The checkout thread reserves with a single atomic conditional update
(UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE count > 0); if no row is updated the customer is told the
item is sold out.

Paying. The payment service charges the customer and marks the order confirmed. It looks the order
up by customer id; whether the hold is still active or has already expired is not checked at this
point (the hold is only a soft guarantee during browsing).

Initially all customers are browsing and the stock count is 4.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state

  (:predicates

    (mode-4)

    (expired ?c - customer)              ; customer's hold expired and its unit went back to stock

    :effect (and (not (browsing ?c)) (read-1 ?c ?q)))

  (:action hold-ages

    :precondition (and (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (hold-age ?c ?t)) (hold-age ?c ?u)))
  (:action expire-hold

    :precondition (and (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t) (hold-limit ?t) (stock ?q) (next-level ?q ?r))
    :effect (and (not (holding ?c)) (not (hold-age ?c ?t)) (not (stock ?q)) (stock ?r) (expired ?c)))

    """Return a / b rounded to the nearest integer; when a / b is exactly halfway between

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 6 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v6. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. To make sure readers never see the old price once an update has started, for each update
the writer first deletes the product's cache entry and then writes the new version to the database.
The reader always stores the value it read after a miss.

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain cache-aside)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

  (:action read-miss
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))
    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))
  (:action fill-cache
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (plain-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action fill-cache-with-lease
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (leased-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty) (lease))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (not (lease)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action abandon-fill
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (reader-has ?v)
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (reader-idle)))
  (:action begin-update-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action begin-delete-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-invalidate ?v)))
  (:action write-db
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-update ?v) (db ?v) (next-version ?v ?w))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (not (db ?v)) (db ?w) (writer-invalidate ?w)))
  (:action invalidate
    :parameters (?v ?x - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache ?x))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (cache ?x)) (not (lease)) (cache-empty) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action invalidate-empty
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (lease)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action finish-after-delete
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-update ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action finish-after-update
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-invalidate ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action observe-stale
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-done) (cache ?v) (db ?w) (older ?v ?w))
    :effect (stale)))
```

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer records the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
table in the payments database. The wallet credit and the id record are written in the same database
transaction, so either both are stored or neither is (a crash before the commit rolls both back).
Before performing a payout the consumer checks the table: if the id is there it skips the payout and
only acknowledges the message.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain queue)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types message consumer tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)      ; the consumer processes every delivery
    (dedup-durable)   ; processed ids are recorded in the database, atomically with the side effect
    (dedup-memory)    ; processed ids are recorded in an in-memory set of the consumer process
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)
    (not-seen ?m - message) (seen ?m - message))

  (:action receive
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?w) (visible ?m) (in-queue ?m) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))
  (:action process-without-dedup
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-and-record-durably
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-durable) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)
                 (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-and-record-in-memory
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-memory) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)
                 (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action skip-duplicate
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-again
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (processed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (processed-twice ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action ack
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (handled ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t))
    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (not (in-queue ?m)) (idle ?w) (acked ?m)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?m - message ?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (hidden ?m ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (hidden ?m ?u)))
  (:action reappear
    :parameters (?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (hidden ?m ?t) (visibility-timeout ?t) (in-queue ?m))
    :effect (and (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (visible ?m)))
  (:action crash-restart
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (handled ?w ?m)
    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (idle ?w)))
  (:action crash-restart-losing-memory
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-memory) (handled ?w ?m) (seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (not (seen ?m)) (not-seen ?m) (idle ?w))))

def bulk_price(unit_cents, qty):
    """Return the price in cents of `qty` items costing `unit_cents` each. The gross

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Double-Charge Vulnerability

Let me trace through the system step by step to find if a violation is reachable.

## Understanding the Vulnerability Path

To reach `(charged-twice o1)`, I need to execute `charge-again`, which requires:
- `(approved o1 ?a)` for some attempt
- `(charged o1)` already true

This means I need **two separate approvals** and **two separate charge actions**.

## Tracing the Event Sequence

Assuming **mode-1** is enabled (which matches the design document's description: "The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request and charges the customer's card"):

**Steps 1-3: First charge**
1. Send attempt a0 → request in flight
2. Provider accepts it (mode-1) → creates approval
3. Provider charges the card → creates response and marks as charged

**Steps 4-6: Timeout and retry mechanism**
4. Response is lost in the network (network unreliability)
5. Client's timer advances to timeout value t1
6. Client times out on a0 and retries with a1 → back to ready state

**Steps 7-9: Second charge (the violation)**
7. Send attempt a1 → new request in flight
8. Provider accepts it again (mode-1: no idempotency tracking)
9. Provider charges the card a second time → reaches `(charged-twice o1)`

## Verification

Let me verify preconditions hold at each step:

- **Step 1**: `(ready o1 a0) ∧ (first-tick t0)` ✓
- **Step 2**: `(mode-1) ∧ (in-flight o1 a0)` ✓
- **Step 3**: `(approved o1 a0) ∧ (uncharged o1)` ✓
- **Step 4**: `(response o1)` ✓
- **Step 5**: `(waiting o1 a0) ∧ (clock o1 t0) ∧ (next-tick t0 t1)` ✓
- **Step 6**: `(waiting o1 a0) ∧ (clock o1 t1) ∧ (timeout-tick t1) ∧ (next-attempt a0 a1)` ✓
- **Step 7**: `(ready o1 a1) ∧ (first-tick t0)` ✓
- **Step 8**: `(mode-1) ∧ (in-flight o1 a1)` ✓
- **Step 9**: `(approved o1 a1) ∧ (charged o1)` ✓

## Root Cause

The design lacks idempotency: the provider has no mechanism to recognize that a1 is a retry of the same order and should not be charged again. Combined with network unreliability (lost responses triggering retries), this creates a double-charge vulnerability.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Distributed Payment System

Let me systematically trace through the system to find if a double charge is possible.

## Key Observations

1. **The vulnerability surface**: The `charge-again` action produces `charged-twice` when:
   - `approved(?o ?a)` AND `charged(?o)` both hold
   - This means two separate attempts must each reach approval state

2. **Mode-1 weakness**: The `accept-2` action (mode-1) approves any request WITHOUT checking the idempotency record:
   - Precondition: `(mode-1) (in-flight ?o ?a)` only
   - Unlike `accept-1` and `accept-3`, it doesn't require `no-record`

3. **Attack pathway**: 
   - First attempt: approve → charge (sets `record`, produces response)
   - Response lost via network failure
   - Client retries second attempt
   - With mode-1, second attempt approves unconditionally
   - Second approval + existing charge state → can trigger `charge-again`

## Concrete Violation Trace

**Initial state**: `ready(o1, a0), no-record(o1), uncharged(o1), mode-1`

1. **(send o1 a0 t0)**: Client sends first attempt
   - State: `waiting(o1, a0), in-flight(o1, a0), clock(o1, t0)`

2. **(accept-2 o1 a0)**: Provider approves (mode-1, no record check!)
   - State: `approved(o1, a0)` added

3. **(charge o1 a0)**: Card charged, record created
   - State: `charged(o1), record(o1), response(o1), ¬no-record(o1)` 

4. **(lose-response o1)**: Network drops response
   - State: `response(o1)` removed, but charge persists

5. **(tick o1 a0 t0 t1)**: Timer advances
   - State: `clock(o1, t1)`

6. **(time-out-and-retry o1 a0 a1 t1)**: Client times out and retries
   - State: `ready(o1, a1)` (removes `waiting` and `clock`)

7. **(send o1 a1 t0)**: Client sends second attempt
   - State: `waiting(o1, a1), in-flight(o1, a1), clock(o1, t0)`

8. **(accept-2 o1 a1)**: Provider AGAIN approves (mode-1 doesn't check record!)
   - State: `approved(o1, a1)` added, `in-flight` removed

   - Precondition satisfied: `approved(o1, a1) ✓` and `charged(o1) ✓`

it at the same time. Each customer's checkout runs on its own server thread; the threads interleave
arbitrarily. A checkout first reserves a unit (a hold), then the customer pays to confirm the
purchase.

Holds are temporary: a hold that is not paid for expires after 2 clock ticks, and the unit goes
back into stock so that another customer can buy it. Customers can be slow to pay; the payment step
may happen at any later time.

Reserving. The checkout thread reserves with a single atomic conditional update
(UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE count > 0); if no row is updated the customer is told the
item is sold out.

Paying. The payment service charges the customer and marks the order confirmed. It looks the order
up by customer id; whether the hold is still active or has already expired is not checked at this
point (the hold is only a soft guarantee during browsing).

Initially all customers are browsing and the stock count is 2.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types customer level tick)
  (:predicates

    (mode-1)
    (mode-4)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-level ?lower ?higher - level)  ; stock level ?higher is one more than ?lower
    (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)
    (hold-limit ?t - tick)               ; hold age at which a hold expires
    ;; --- state ---
    (stock ?q - level)                   ; current stock level
    (browsing ?c - customer)             ; customer has not started checkout
    (read-1 ?c - customer ?q - level)
    (holding ?c - customer)              ; customer holds one reserved unit
    (hold-age ?c - customer ?t - tick)
    (expired ?c - customer)              ; customer's hold expired and its unit went back to stock
    (sold ?c - customer))                ; customer's purchase is confirmed

  (:action read-1
    :parameters (?c - customer ?q ?p - level)
    :precondition (and (mode-1) (browsing ?c) (stock ?q) (next-level ?p ?q))
    :effect (and (not (browsing ?c)) (read-1 ?c ?q)))
  (:action write-stock

    :precondition (and (read-1 ?c ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (stock ?cur) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (read-1 ?c ?q)) (not (stock ?cur)) (stock ?p) (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t)))
  (:action reserve-1

    :precondition (and (mode-4) (browsing ?c) (stock ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (browsing ?c)) (not (stock ?q)) (stock ?p) (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t)))

    :effect (and (not (hold-age ?c ?t)) (hold-age ?c ?u)))

## Understanding the System

The design uses:
- **Atomic reserve** via `reserve-1` action (mode-4): `UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE count > 0`
- **Payment without expiration checks**: "whether the hold is still active or has already expired is not checked at this point"
- **Hold expiration**: after 2 clock ticks, returns unit to stock

The design description explicitly states that payment proceeds regardless of hold status, and customers can pay at any later time—this implies both `pay` (while holding) and `pay-1` (after hold expired, mode-2) are allowed.

## Critical Vulnerability

The key issue: **holds can expire and return units to stock, while the expired customer can still pay later**. This allows selling the same unit twice.

## Trace

Starting from initial state with:
- `(stock q2)`, `(browsing c1)`, `(browsing c2)`, `(browsing c3)`
- All static facts: `next-level`, `next-tick`, `zero-tick`, `hold-limit t2`
- Modes: `(mode-4)` and `(mode-2)` (per design description)

- `(reserve-1 c1 q2 q1 t0)` → c1 holds, stock → q1

**2. Reserve c2:**
- `(reserve-1 c2 q1 q0 t0)` → c2 holds, stock → q0

**3-4. Age c1's hold to expiration:**
- `(hold-ages c1 t0 t1)` → age t0 → t1
- `(hold-ages c1 t1 t2)` → age t1 → t2

**5. c1's hold expires, unit returns to stock:**
- `(expire-hold c1 t2 q0 q1)` → stock → q1, c1 now expired

**6. c2 pays (still holding):**
- `(pay c2 t0)` → c2 sold

**7. c3 reserves the returned unit:**
- `(reserve-1 c3 q1 q0 t0)` → c3 holds, stock → q0

**8. c3 pays:**
- `(pay c3 t0)` → c3 sold

**9. c1 pays after expiration (mode-2 allows this):**
- `(pay-1 c1)` → c1 sold

Final state has `(sold c1)`, `(sold c2)`, `(sold c3)` — **all three customers confirmed**, despite only 2 units in stock.

1. c1's unit is reserved, then expires and returns to stock
2. c3 re-reserves that same unit

Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 3 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v3. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry, so the next read misses and loads the new version. The reader always
stores the value it read after a miss.

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete

Let me trace through the system carefully, using the design specification: **update-then-delete** (writer updates DB then deletes cache) and **plain-set** (reader always stores what it reads).

The key insight is that the reader can be delayed arbitrarily between reading the database and storing in the cache. Here's an event sequence that violates safety:

**The Critical Scenario:**

1. **Writer starts update v0→v1**: (begin-update-first v0)
2. **Reader issues cache miss**: (read-miss v0) — reads v0 from DB, gets a lease, holds the value
3. **Writer writes v1 to DB**: (write-db v0 v1) — database now at v1
4. **Writer invalidates**: (invalidate-empty v1) — cache is empty anyway, writer continues
5. **Writer writes v2 to DB**: (write-db v1 v2) — database now at v2
6. **Writer invalidates**: (invalidate-empty v2) — cache empty, writer continues
7. **Writer writes v3 to DB**: (write-db v2 v3) — database now at v3
8. **Writer invalidates**: (invalidate-empty v3) — cache empty, writer finishes
9. **Writer completes**: (finish-after-delete v3) — writer-done
10. **Reader fills cache with stale data**: (fill-cache v0) — reader finally stores v0 (the value it read in step 2), cache now holds v0

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain payments)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

  (:action send
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-no-dedup
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))
                 (charged ?o) (record ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (response ?o))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (response ?o)) (confirmed ?o)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (clock ?o ?t)) (clock ?o ?u)))
  (:action time-out-and-retry
    :parameters (?o - order ?a ?b - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (timeout-tick ?t) (next-attempt ?a ?b))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (clock ?o ?t)) (ready ?o ?b))))

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 3 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    (mode-4)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Lease-Lock Design

I'll work through the event space systematically to determine if corruption is reachable.

## Design Interpretation

The problem describes:
- **Storage behavior**: "The storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only" → `(no-fencing)`
- **Worker behavior**: "they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired the lock keeps believing it holds it" → `(no-lease-check)`

These are implicit design choices in the specification.

## Attack Sequence

The vulnerability exploits the gap between when a lease expires and when a stalled worker wakes up:

1. **c1 acquires the lock** with token k1, expecting a 11-tick lease
2. **Time passes**: 11 ticks advance (t0→t1→...→t11)
3. **Lease expires**: At t11, the lock service expires c1's lease
4. **c1 remains stalled** but still believes it holds the lock (key: it learned nothing about expiry)
5. **c2 acquires the lock** with token k2 and writes successfully
6. **c1 wakes up**: It still believes it holds the lock (no lease check before write)
7. **c1 writes with old token**: Since there's no fencing, storage accepts the write with token k1 over c2's write with k2
8. **Corruption**: An older token's write was applied after a newer token's write

  - `(wrote k2)` ✓ (c2 successfully wrote)
  - `(token-less k1 k2)` ✓ (k1 issued before k2, static fact)

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t11 (11 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain payments)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside

the database from version v0 to v4. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.

the writer first deletes the product's cache entry and then writes the new version to the database.
The reader always stores the value it read after a miss.

    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database

    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file

lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 11 clock ticks, after which the lock service

slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The

# Analysis: Pre-Mortem on Leader Lock Design

Looking at this distributed system, I need to find if there's a concrete event sequence where an expired lease holder's write is applied after an active holder's write, reaching the `(corrupted)` state.

## Key Observations

1. **Lease Expiry Doesn't Clear Belief**: When a lease expires via the `expire` action, the holder's `(believes)` fact is NOT removed—only `(holder)` is cleared. A stalled worker continues believing it holds the lock indefinitely.

2. **Mode-4 Enables Dangerous Writes**: The `prepare-1` action requires only `(believes ?c)` (not `(holder ?c)`) when mode-4 is active. This allows an expired-lease holder to reach `(may-write)`.

3. **Mode-2 Detects but Doesn't Prevent**: The `write-1` action in mode-2 allows writing an older token after a newer one—it simply marks the result as corrupted.

## Concrete Violation Sequence

Here's how corruption becomes reachable:

1. **c1 acquires lease with token k1** → c1 believes it holds the lock
2. **Lease ages and expires** → c1 no longer holds the lock, but still believes it does  
3. **c2 acquires lease with token k2** (a newer token)
4. **c2 writes with k2** (current holder writes)
5. **c1 (expired holder) writes with k1** → older token written after newer token
6. **Result**: `(corrupted)` flag is set

### Event Sequence

```
(acquire c1 k0 k1 t0)     ; c1 gets lock and token k1
(tick t0 t1)              ; time advances
(tick t1 t2)
(tick t2 t3)
(tick t3 t4)
(tick t4 t5)
(tick t5 t6)
(tick t6 t7)              ; lease age reaches limit
(expire c1 t7)            ; c1's lease expires, but c1 still believes!
(acquire c2 k1 k2 t0)     ; c2 gets lock and newer token k2
(prepare-1 c2)            ; [requires mode-4] c2 prepares to write
(write-4 c2 k2)           ; [requires mode-2] c2 writes with k2
(prepare-1 c1)            ; [requires mode-4] c1 prepares (c1 still believes!)
(write-1 c1 k1 k2)        ; [requires mode-2] c1 writes k1 after k2 → CORRUPTED
```

The final action `(write-1 c1 k1 k2)` has preconditions:
- `(mode-2)` ✓ assumed
- `(may-write c1)` ✓ set by step 13
- `(token-of c1 k1)` ✓ set by step 1
- `(wrote k2)` ✓ set by step 12
- `(token-less k1 k2)` ✓ static fact

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Double Charge Vulnerability

Let me work through this systematically to find if `(charged-twice o1)` can be reached.

## Key Observations

To reach `(charged-twice o1)`, I need to trigger the `charge-again` action, which requires:
- `(approved ?o ?a)` for some attempt
- `(charged ?o)` already true

The only way `(charged o1)` becomes true is via the `charge` action (when `(uncharged o1)` is true). Then, if I can get a *second* approval while `(charged o1)` persists, I can call `charge-again`.

## The Vulnerability: Mode-1

Looking at the provider's accept logic:
- **accept-1** (mode-3): requires `(no-record o1)`, removes it when approving
- **accept-3** (mode-2): requires `(no-record o1)` when approving  
- **accept-2** (mode-1): **has no idempotency check** — it approves any request

In mode-1, the provider accepts requests *without verifying the idempotency table*. This is the vulnerability.

## Exploit Sequence

1. **Send attempt a0** — request enters network
2. **accept-2 a0** (mode-1) — provider accepts without checking record
3. **charge a0** — card charged, record stored, response generated
4. **lose-response** — response lost in network
5. **Timeout a0** (tick 7 times, then time-out-and-retry) — client gives up and retries
6. **Send attempt a1** — new request enters network  
7. **accept-2 a1** (mode-1) — provider accepts AGAIN without checking record
8. **charge-again a1** — **card charged a second time**

The response loss at step 4 is crucial: it prevents the client from confirming, triggering the retry mechanism. Meanwhile, mode-1's lack of idempotency checking means the provider approves the retried request as if it were new.

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t15 (15 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state

  (:types order attempt tick)

    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---

    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt

    ;; --- network ---

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number

waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t3 (3 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds

I'll work through this systematically to find if there's an event sequence that violates the safety requirement.

## Initial State
- Stock: q3 (3 units)
- Customers: c1, c2, c3, c4 all browsing
- Static facts: mode-1, mode-4, mode-2, mode-3 all enabled (per PDDL domain)
- Ticks: t0 is the initial tick; hold-limit is t3

## Exploit Analysis

The critical issue is a **check-then-act race condition** in the `write-stock` action:

```

  :precondition (and (read-1 ?c ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (stock ?cur) (zero-tick ?t))
  :effect (and (not (read-1 ?c ?q)) (not (stock ?cur)) (stock ?p) (holding ?c) (hold-age ?c ?t)))
```

This action does **not verify** that the current stock `?cur` matches the stock level `?q` that was read. This allows multiple customers to:
1. All read the same stock level (q3)
2. All subsequently execute `write-stock` with their stale reads
3. All successfully obtain holdings despite insufficient stock

## Violation Trace

Here's a concrete event sequence that causes all 4 customers to be sold out (violating the invariant):

**Phase 1: Racy Read (all customers read the initial level)**
1. All four customers read stock=q3 before any writes happen
2. `(read-1 c1 q3)` — c1 reads stock
3. `(read-1 c2 q3)` — c2 reads stock  
4. `(read-1 c3 q3)` — c3 reads stock
5. `(read-1 c4 q3)` — c4 reads stock

**Phase 2: Racy Write (all execute write-stock at their leisure)**
6. `(write-stock c1 q3 q2 q3 t0)` — stock: q3 → q2, c1 gets holding
7. `(write-stock c2 q3 q2 q2 t0)` — stock: q2 → q2 (idempotent), c2 gets holding
8. `(write-stock c3 q3 q2 q2 t0)` — stock: q2 → q2 (idempotent), c3 gets holding
9. `(write-stock c4 q3 q2 q2 t0)` — stock: q2 → q2 (idempotent), c4 gets holding

**Result after Phase 2:**
- All 4 customers have `(holding ?c)` and `(hold-age ?c t0)`
- Only 1 unit actually reserved (stock went q3 → q2)

10. `(pay c1 t0)` — c1 gets (sold c1)
11. `(pay c2 t0)` — c2 gets (sold c2)
12. `(pay c3 t0)` — c3 gets (sold c3)
13. `(pay c4 t0)` — c4 gets (sold c4)

# Pre-Mortem Analysis: Stock Reservation Design

Let me work through this systematically, examining whether the system's atomic update guarantee can be violated.

## Key Observations

1. **The read-1 action** records what stock level a customer observed, but doesn't acquire exclusivity
2. **The write-stock action** has a critical vulnerability: it takes parameters `?q` (what was read) and `?cur` (current stock level), treating them independently

The `write-stock` action is:
```pddl
:precondition (and (read-1 ?c ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (stock ?cur) (zero-tick ?t))
:effect (and (not (stock ?cur)) (stock ?p) (holding ?c) ...)
```

Where `next-level ?p ?q` means `p = q - 1`.

**The bug:** The action removes whatever `?cur` is and adds `?p`. When multiple customers read the same level and execute writes in sequence:
- Customer 1 reads q4, writes with cur=q4, p=q3: stock q4 → q3 ✓ (decrements)
- Customer 2 reads q4, writes with cur=q3, p=q3: stock q3 → q3 (no decrement!)  
- Customers 3-5 do the same: stock stays at q3

All 5 customers become `holding` but stock only decreased once.

Starting from: `stock q4`, all customers browsing

(read-1 c2 q4 q3)

(read-1 c4 q4 q3)
(read-1 c5 q4 q3)

(write-stock c3 q4 q3 q3 t0)
(write-stock c4 q4 q3 q3 t0)
(write-stock c5 q4 q3 q3 t0)
(pay c1 t0)
(pay c2 t0)
(pay c3 t0)

not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

table in the payments database. The payout ledger entry and the id record are written in the same

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside

on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 2 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v2. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. To make sure readers never see the old price once an update has started, for each update
the writer first deletes the product's cache entry and then writes the new version to the database.

Looking at this pre-mortem, I need to identify a concrete event sequence that leads to the cache holding an older version than the database after the writer finishes.

Let me trace through the system carefully.

## Key observations

1. The reader can be delayed arbitrarily between reading the database and storing in the cache
2. The writer's strategy is to delete cache THEN write DB (safety-first invalidation)
3. Cache entries never expire, so stale data persists indefinitely
4. The writer has two updates: v0→v1→v2

## The vulnerability

The problem is a **time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race**:
- The reader reads v0 from the database (at some early point)
- The reader hasn't yet stored v0 in the cache (delayed)
- The writer progresses through all updates: v0→v1→v2
- The writer finishes its work
- The reader finally fills the cache with v0
- Result: cache has v0, database has v2, writer is done → **stale!**

## Event sequence

Assume initial state plus: `(mode-3)` (writer invalidates first) and `(mode-2)` (reader uses fill-1).

1. `(read-miss v0)` — Reader reads v0 from DB during cache miss
   - State: reader-has v0, lease set, cache-empty

2. `(begin-2 v0)` — Writer begins, moves to invalidate first (mode-3)
   - State: writer-invalidate v0

3. `(invalidate-empty v0)` — Writer invalidates cache (already empty)
   - State: writer-update v0 (lease cleared)

4. `(write-db v0 v1)` — Writer writes v1 to database
   - State: db v1, writer-invalidate v1

5. `(invalidate-empty v1)` — Writer invalidates (still empty)
   - State: writer-update v1

6. `(write-db v1 v2)` — Writer writes v2 to database
   - State: db v2, writer-invalidate v2

7. `(finish-1 v2)` — Writer finishes (mode-3, has writer-invalidate v2 at final version)
   - State: writer-done, db v2

8. `(fill-1 v0)` — Reader finally fills cache with the v0 it read earlier
   - State: cache v0, db v2, writer-done

9. `(observe-stale v0 v2)` — Observation confirms: cache v0 < db v2 with writer-done
   - State: **stale** ✓

The violation occurs because the reader captures v0 early, then the writer invalidates cache and advances to v2, and finally the reader stores its stale v0 into the cache after the writer completes.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t5 (5 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

    ;; --- static counters ---

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 6 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v6. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database

    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---

# Pre-mortem Code Review: triangle_kind

Let me carefully analyze this function against its specification.

## Key Issue: Logic Error in Invalid Triangle Detection

The specification states: **"Return 0 if they do not form a valid triangle, meaning some side is greater than or equal to the sum of the other two."**

This means an invalid triangle occurs when:
- a ≥ b + c **OR**
- b ≥ a + c **OR**  
- c ≥ a + b

(At least ONE of these conditions must hold)

## The Bug

The code uses:
```python
if a + b <= c and a + c <= b and (b + c <= a):
    return 0
```

This checks if **ALL THREE** conditions are simultaneously true (using `and`), which is **mathematically impossible** for positive numbers:
- If `a + c <= b`, then b ≥ a + c
- If `b + c <= a`, then a ≥ b + c

Combined: a ≥ b + c ≥ (a + c) + c = a + 2c, implying 0 ≥ 2c, which is impossible.

The condition should use `or` instead of `and`.

## Concrete Failing Input

**Input: a=1, b=2, c=3**

- Valid triangle check: 1 + 2 = 3, so c = a + b (invalid triangle ✓)
- **Expected**: 0 (per docstring: "some side is greater than or equal to the sum of the other two")
- **Code execution**:
  - First condition: `(3 <= 3) and (4 <= 2) and (5 <= 1)` = `True and False and False` = `False`
  - Doesn't return 0
  - Sides aren't all equal (return 3) ✗
  - Sides aren't exactly two equal (return 2) ✗
  - Returns 1
- **Actual**: 1

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 1 clock tick, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    (mode-4)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with mode-3)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

  (:action acquire
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?l - token ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?c) (lock-free) (last-issued ?k) (next-token ?k ?l) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)
                 (holder ?c) (believes ?c) (token-of ?c ?l) (lease-age ?t)))
  (:action tick

- **write-2** (mode-3): Similar in mode-3 with max-seen tracking

I'll assume both **mode-2** and **mode-4** are active initially (the domain allows independent mode predicates).

Let me trace through an execution:

1. **acquire(c1, k0, k1, t0)**: c1 acquires lock with token k1

   - Sets: `may-write(c1)`

3. **tick(t0, t1)**: Time advances

4. **expire(c1, t1)**: Lock service expires c1's lease

   - **But keeps**: `believes(c1), token-of(c1, k1), may-write(c1)` (stale beliefs!)

5. **acquire(c2, k1, k2, t0)**: c2 acquires lock with token k2
   - Pre: `idle(c2), lock-free, last-issued(k1), next-token(k1, k2), zero-tick(t0)` ✓
   - Sets: `holder(c2), believes(c2), token-of(c2, k2), lease-age(t0)`

   - Sets: `wrote(k2)`

8. **write-1(c1, k1, k2)**: c1 writes with expired lease
   - Pre: `mode-2, may-write(c1), token-of(c1, k1), wrote(k2), token-less(k1, k2)` ✓

- `(not-seen ?m)` - the message is NOT in the consumer's dedup set

   - **But the `processed(m1)` flag persists, and message stays in queue!**

   - Message age increments through the visibility timeout window
   - Message remains hidden but unacknowledged

5. **reappear**: After 7 ticks, message visibility timeout expires
   - Message becomes visible again and re-queues

   - Sets `working(w1,m1)=true`

   - `working(w1,m1)=true` (from step 6)

Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 2 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v2. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry, so the next read misses and loads the new version. The reader always
stores the value it read after a miss.

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))
    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))

  (:action fill-cache-with-lease

    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (not (lease)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))

I'll trace through the event model systematically to find if a double charge can occur.

Looking at the design document, the key facts are:
- The provider **does not deduplicate requests** ("the provider does not use it to detect repeats")

can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.

the product's cache entry, so the next read misses and loads the new version. The reader always
stores the value it read after a miss.

    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Stock Reservation System

Let me trace through this distributed system to find event sequences that could violate the safety property (selling more units than in stock).

## Initial State
- `stock: q2`
- `browsing: {c1, c2, c3}`
- All other predicates false
- Clock at `t0`

## The Vulnerability

I'll examine the **racy read-1 + write-stock path** (mode-1). The critical flaw is in the `write-stock` precondition:

```pddl
:precondition (and (read-1 ?c ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (stock ?cur) (zero-tick ?t))
```

This checks that:
- Customer read some level `?q` ✓
- We can decrement to `?p` ✓  
- **There exists some stock level `?cur`** ← This doesn't verify that `?cur == ?q` !
- It's time `t0` ✓

The bug: **`write-stock` doesn't verify the stock level hasn't changed since the read!**

## Attack Sequence

**Steps 1-3: All three customers read stock level q2**
```
read-1 c1 q2 q1   → (read-1 c1 q2)
read-1 c2 q2 q1   → (read-1 c2 q2)  
read-1 c3 q2 q1   → (read-1 c3 q2)
```
All customers see 2 units available.

**Step 4: c1 decrements the stock**
```
write-stock c1 q2 q1 q2 t0
  Precondition: (read-1 c1 q2)✓, (next-level q1 q2)✓, (stock q2)✓, (zero-tick t0)✓
  Effect: stock q2 → q1, (holding c1) added
```
Stock is now q1. One unit reserved.

**Step 5: c2 attempts write-stock (with q1 as current stock)**
```
write-stock c2 q2 q1 q1 t0
  Precondition: (read-1 c2 q2)✓, (next-level q1 q2)✓, (stock q1)✓, (zero-tick t0)✓
  Effect: (not (stock q1)) and (stock q1) → STOCK UNCHANGED!
         But: (holding c2) is ADDED
```
The precondition binds `?cur=q1`. The effect removes q1 and re-adds q1, so stock stays q1. **But c2 becomes holding without actually reserving!**

**Step 6: c3 does the same**
```
write-stock c3 q2 q1 q1 t0
  Precondition: (read-1 c3 q2)✓, (next-level q1 q2)✓, (stock q1)✓, (zero-tick t0)✓
  Effect: stock q1 → q1 (unchanged), (holding c3) added
```

**Steps 7-9: All three pay and confirm**
```
pay c1 t0  → (sold c1)
pay c2 t0  → (sold c2)
pay c3 t0  → (sold c3)
```

All three customers end up with `(sold c1)`, `(sold c2)`, `(sold c3)` **despite only 2 units being in stock.**

external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in

several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up

timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t11 (11 ticks after sending)

waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds

- Fail precondition checks if `max-seen > token`, or  
- Still fail because writing an old token over a newer token would require an impossible token ordering

# Analysis: Can the payout be performed twice?

Looking at this design, I need to trace through the event model to find a scenario where `(processed-twice m1)` becomes true.

## Key Observations

1. **Deduplication modes**: The design document doesn't explicitly specify deduplication, but the PDDL includes three modes. The minimal interpretation is `dedup-none`, which performs no deduplication.

2. **Critical vulnerability**: If the consumer crashes after calling the bank API (performing the payout) but *before* acknowledging the message, the message will remain unacknowledged. After the 7-tick visibility timeout, it reappears and will be redelivered.

3. **Persistent facts**: The `(zero-tick t0)` predicate is never removed from the state, so `receive` can be called multiple times with the same tick parameter.

## Violation Trace

Starting from initial state:
- `(in-queue m1) (visible m1) (idle w1) (unprocessed m1) (not-seen m1) (dedup-none)`
- `(zero-tick t0) (next-tick t0 t1) ... (next-tick t6 t7) (visibility-timeout t7)`

**Steps 1–2:** Process the first delivery normally
1. `(receive w1 m1 t0)` — Consumer receives and hides the message
2. `(process-without-dedup w1 m1)` — **Payout executed**, marked as `(processed m1)` and `(handled w1 m1)`

**Step 3:** Crash before acknowledgment
3. `(crash-restart w1 m1)` — Consumer crashes; message remains in queue, still hidden, but no longer handled. **Payout already made but not acknowledged.**

**Steps 4–10:** Time advances until visibility timeout
4. `(tick m1 t0 t1)` — Message ages
5. `(tick m1 t1 t2)`
6. `(tick m1 t2 t3)`
7. `(tick m1 t3 t4)`
8. `(tick m1 t4 t5)`
9. `(tick m1 t5 t6)`
10. `(tick m1 t6 t7)` — Message reaches visibility timeout age

**Step 11:** Message reappears
11. `(reappear m1 t7)` — Message becomes visible again (timeout triggered)

**Step 12:** Consumer receives the same message again
12. `(receive w1 m1 t0)` — `(zero-tick t0)` still holds, so this is valid. Message hidden again.

13. `(process-again w1 m1)` — Since `(processed m1)` is true but `(not-seen m1)` is true (dedup-none never records what was processed), this action fires, setting `(processed-twice m1)`.

--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 1 clock tick, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 2 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v2. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry, so the next read misses and loads the new version. The reader always
stores the value it read after a miss.

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain cache-aside)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

  (:action read-miss
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))
    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))
  (:action fill-cache

The system provides two design options:
- **update-then-delete**: writer updates DB, then invalidates cache
- **delete-then-update**: writer invalidates cache, then updates DB

And two reader storage options:
- **plain-set**: reader stores its value unconditionally  
- **leased-set**: reader stores only if its lease was never revoked

## Finding the Violation

With **plain-set** + **update-then-delete**, I can construct a violation:

1. Writer writes v1 to DB, then invalidates cache (which is empty, revoking any lease)
