--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t15 (15 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain payments)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

  (:action send
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-no-dedup
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))
                 (charged ?o) (record ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (response ?o))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (response ?o)) (confirmed ?o)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (clock ?o ?t)) (clock ?o ?u)))
  (:action time-out-and-retry
    :parameters (?o - order ?a ?b - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (timeout-tick ?t) (next-attempt ?a ?b))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (clock ?o ?t)) (ready ?o ?b))))
```

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

  (:action send
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-no-dedup
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))
                 (charged ?o) (record ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (response ?o))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (response ?o)) (confirmed ?o)))
  (:action tick

    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (clock ?o ?t)) (clock ?o ?u)))

    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (clock ?o ?t)) (ready ?o ?b))))

The critical flaw is in the **non-atomic read-then-write** sequence in the `read-1` and `write-stock` actions:

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 2 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v2. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state

    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)

    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging. The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request
and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 3 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Once a worker holds the lock it writes the file. The storage service accepts any write;
the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

  (:requirements :strips :typing)

    (mode-2)

    (mode-4)

    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)

    ;; --- storage ---

Looking at this system, I need to find whether an event sequence can lead to the `(corrupted)` predicate being true—meaning an older token write gets applied after a newer token write.

## Analysis of the Vulnerability

The key vulnerability here is the **gap between lease checking and writing**:

1. A worker checks it holds the lease (action: `check-lease-and-prepare-write`)
2. The worker prepares to write but then **stalls** (can stall indefinitely per the design)
3. While stalled, the lease **expires** (15 clock ticks pass)
4. Another worker acquires the lock and writes with a **newer token**
5. The first worker wakes up and writes with its **older token**, corrupting the file

The problem states: "Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time... and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired the lock keeps believing it holds it."

The design's lease checking (`checks-lease`) alone cannot prevent this because the check happens before the stall, not right before the write itself. With `no-fencing` (storage accepts any write), there's no mechanism to reject the stale token.

## Event Sequence

Here's the concrete attack:

1. Worker c1 acquires the lock with token k1
2. c1 checks its lease—it still holds it—and prepares to write
3. c1 stalls while time ticks forward 15 times (until lease expires at t15)
4. The lock service expires c1's lease, lock becomes free
5. Worker c2 acquires the lock with token k2
6. c2 checks its lease, prepares to write, and writes with k2
7. c1 wakes up from stall and writes with k1 (older token), overwriting k2's write

This sets `(corrupted)` because `write-unfenced-over-newer` fires with k1 < k2.

Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 1 clock tick, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed

lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The

calling the bank API (an external side effect that cannot be undone), then acknowledges the message

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 5 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it performs the payout, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 4 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v4. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-4)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)

    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))

# Analysis of Distributed System Design

Let me work through this carefully, step-by-step, to determine if the safety requirement can be violated.

## Understanding the Initial State

Based on the design document:
- **Reservation mechanism**: "atomic conditional update" → `(stock-atomic)` is true
- **Payment mechanism**: "not checked at this point" → `(pay-ignores-hold)` is true  
- **Initial state**: 8 units in stock, 9 browsing customers

So the initial state includes:
- `(stock-atomic)`
- `(pay-ignores-hold)` 
- `(stock q8)`
- `(browsing c1)` through `(browsing c9)`

## Critical Constraint: The Zero-Tick Precondition

Both the `reserve-atomic` and `write-stock` actions have the precondition `(zero-tick ?t)`:

```pddl
(:action reserve-atomic
  :parameters (?c - customer ?q ?p - level ?t - tick)
  :precondition (and (stock-atomic) (browsing ?c) (stock ?q) (next-level ?p ?q) (zero-tick ?t))
```

In STRIPS, `(zero-tick ?t)` is only true when `?t = t0` (the initial tick). This means **all reservation attempts must occur at time t0**. Once time progresses to t1, no more reserves are possible.

## Analyzing Atomic Reservation

With `(stock-atomic)` enabled:

1. **At t0**: Customers c1 through c8 can each successfully execute `reserve-atomic`:
   - c1: `(reserve-atomic c1 q8 q7 t0)` → stock: q8→q7
   - c2: `(reserve-atomic c2 q7 q6 t0)` → stock: q7→q6
   - ...
   - c8: `(reserve-atomic c8 q1 q0 t0)` → stock: q1→q0

2. **c9's reserve attempt fails**: After 8 reserves, stock is q0. The precondition `(stock ?q)` with `(next-level ?p ?q)` requires a level q where q > 0. Since only q0 is available and `(next-level ?p q0)` has no solution (would need p = -1), c9 cannot reserve.

## Can c9 Become Sold Another Way?

To reach `(sold c9)`, c9 must either:
- Execute `pay`: requires `(holding c9)` — but c9 never reserved
- Execute `pay-after-expiry`: requires `(expired c9)` — but to become expired, c9 must have been holding first

Since c9 never holds, there is no path for c9 to become sold.

## Verification of Maximum Sales

- Maximum customers who can hold: 8 (one per unit, all reserves at t0)
- All 8 holding customers can later either:
  - Pay via `pay` action while holding
  - Wait for hold to expire via `expire-hold`, then pay via `pay-after-expiry`
- Therefore, maximum confirmed purchases: 8

## Conclusion

With the atomic reservation design and `pay-ignores-hold` mechanism as described, it is **impossible** for all 9 customers to end up with confirmed purchases. The system maintains its safety property.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t5 (5 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response

    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))

    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))

1. **The violation requires**: `(charge-again)` to fire, which needs:
   - `(approved ?o ?a)` — some attempt has been approved
   - `(charged ?o)` — the order has already been charged once

2. **Two successful charges happen if**:

   - Second attempt reaches `approved` again → then `charge-again` can fire

2. Charge succeeds, response is lost in transit
3. Client times out (7 ticks pass without receiving the response)
4. Client retries with attempt a1
5. Attempt a1 is also approved (no deduplication check!)
6. A second charge fires via `charge-again`

}
```

**Explanation**: The charge succeeds but the response is lost before the client receives it. The client times out and retries. I need to find a concrete event sequence where `processed-twice(m1)` becomes true, which would mean the payout executes twice—a safety violation.

Examining the action definitions, I notice:

   - Effect: Sets `processed-twice(?m)`

   - Precondition: mode-1, `handled(?w, ?m)`, `seen(?m)`
   - Effect: Sets `not-seen(?m)` (removes `seen(?m)`)

Here's the attack chain:

1. **First processing**: Receive → Process (marking it processed and seen) → **Crash before acknowledging**

3. **Second processing**: Receive the same message again → Call `process-again` (because it's now processed-but-not-seen after the crash reset)

   - `(processed m1)`: m1 has already been processed

1. **First receive**: Consumer w1 receives m1 (from queue, at t0)

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

The violation occurs via the `charge-again` action, which requires:
- `(approved ?o ?a)` - a request is approved

So I need to construct a scenario where **two different attempts are approved, but the second charge happens after the first completes**.

The vulnerability exists in **dedup-racy mode** because there's a window between when a request lookup succeeds (before charge) and when the idempotency record is written (after charge):

**Event sequence:**

1. **send o1 a0 t0** — Client sends attempt a0
2. **accept-new-racy o1 a0** — Provider looks up o1, finds no record (✓ passes dedup check), approves a0
3. **tick o1 a0 t0 t1** — Client timer advances
4. **time-out-and-retry o1 a0 a1 t1** — Client times out on a0, becomes ready for a1
   - *Still holding*: `(approved o1 a0)`, `(no-record o1)`, `(uncharged o1)`
5. **send o1 a1 t0** — Client sends attempt a1 (reuses first-tick t0)
6. **accept-new-racy o1 a1** — Provider looks up o1 again, STILL finds no record (charge for a0 hasn't executed yet), approves a1
   - *Now we have*: `(approved o1 a0)`, `(approved o1 a1)`, `(no-record o1)`, `(uncharged o1)`
7. **charge o1 a0** — Provider charges for a0, writes idempotency record

8. **charge-again o1 a1** — Provider charges a1 because it's still approved
   - **Violation**: `(charged-twice o1)` is set ✗

This works because in racy deduplication mode, the provider doesn't atomically reserve the key—it only checks for a record and later writes it after charging. A0 and A1 can both pass the lookup (no record exists when both check) before either one writes the record.

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 4 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v4. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Cache-Aside Product Page System

Looking for event sequences that produce `(stale)`: writer finished with cache holding an older version than the database.

## Key Observations

The `(stale)` fact can only be asserted by the `observe-stale` action, which requires:
- `(writer-done)` – writer has completed all updates
- `(cache ?v)` and `(db ?w)` – both cache and DB hold versions
- `(older ?v ?w)` – cache version is older than database version

## Vulnerability Analysis

The critical insight is that the system supports two reader strategies:
1. **`(plain-set)`** – reader stores cache values whenever it wants, without lease validation
2. **`(leased-set)`** – reader stores only if lease is still valid

With **`plain-set`** semantics combined with **`update-then-delete`** writer strategy, a race condition emerges:

The reader can perform `read-miss(v0)` very early, acquiring `(reader-has v0)`, then hold that value through the entire write sequence. Meanwhile, the writer updates v0→v1→v2→v3→v4. After the writer finishes via `finish-after-delete`, the reader can still perform `fill-cache(v0)` because `plain-set` imposes no lease requirement. At that point the cache contains an old value while the database is at v4.

## Event Sequence

Starting from: `{db(v0), cache-empty, reader-idle, writer-update(v0), update-then-delete, plain-set}`

```
(read-miss v0)           → reader-has(v0), lease created
(write-db v0 v1)         → db(v1), writer-invalidate(v1)
(invalidate-empty v1)    → writer-update(v1), cache still empty
(write-db v1 v2)         → db(v2), writer-invalidate(v2)
(invalidate-empty v2)    → writer-update(v2), cache still empty
(write-db v2 v3)         → db(v3), writer-invalidate(v3)
(invalidate-empty v3)    → writer-update(v3), cache still empty
(write-db v3 v4)         → db(v4), writer-invalidate(v4)
(invalidate-empty v4)    → writer-update(v4), writer ready to finish
(finish-after-delete v4) → writer-done (WRITER FINISHED)
(fill-cache v0)          → cache(v0) NOW WITH v0 WHILE db(v4)
(observe-stale v0 v4)    → stale (VIOLATION)
```

Each action's precondition holds at the moment of execution, and the final state satisfies `(writer-done) ∧ (stale)`.

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Checkout Payment Flow

Let me trace through this system carefully to look for concrete event sequences that violate the safety requirement (no double-charging).

## Key Observations

The safety violation occurs when `(charged-twice o1)` becomes true. This requires:
1. First charge via the `charge` action: consumes `(approved ?a)` + `(uncharged o1)` → produces `(charged o1)`
2. Second charge via `charge-again` action: consumes `(approved ?a')` + `(charged o1)` → produces `(charged-twice o1)`

So I need **two different attempts to be approved while handling a delayed/lost response**.

## Vulnerability in dedup-none Mode

The design document explicitly states: *"The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment... the provider does not use it to detect repeats."* This corresponds to the `dedup-none` mode in the PDDL.

Under this mode, `accept-no-dedup` will approve ANY arriving request, regardless of whether we've already charged for this order.

## Event Sequence

Here's a concrete trace that achieves double-charging:

1. Client sends attempt a0 with fresh timer
2. Provider immediately accepts a0 (no dedup check)
3. Provider charges the card (first charge) and loses the response
4. Client's timer expires after 7 ticks with no response received
5. Client retries with attempt a1
6. Provider accepts a1 (still no dedup—nothing prevents this)
7. Provider charges again for a1 (second charge) ✗ **Violation**

The critical vulnerability: after the first charge succeeds, the response is lost in transit before the client can receive it. The client times out and retries. The provider, having no deduplication mechanism, approves and charges the retry as a completely new payment. No idempotency record was written before the first charge response was lost, so there's no data structure to prevent the second charge.

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file

lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 7 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,

the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t11 (11 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

  (:types order attempt tick)

    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response

    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---

    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))

    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge

    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))

  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response

  (:action receive-response

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside

can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.

transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on

without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

    ;; --- static counters ---

    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

def longest_streak(xs):
    """Return the length of the longest run of equal values in consecutive positions of
    `xs` (a single element is a run of length 1). Return 0 for an empty list.

    if not xs:
        return 0
    best = 1
    run = 1
    for i in range(1, len(xs)):

            run += 1
            if run > best:

        else:

    return best

- Worker c2 acquires lock with token k2, writes it
- c1 still *believes* it holds the lock (expire doesn't remove believes)

(tick t0 t1)

(prepare-1 c2)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in

waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

## Understanding the Violation Mechanism

The `charge-again` action is the key to reaching the violation:
```

:precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
:effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o))

For this to fire, we need:
1. The card already charged once: `(charged o1)`
2. A second approval pending: `(approved o1 a1)` or later

The critical insight is that **multiple attempts can be approved simultaneously** if they arrive at the provider before state changes serialize them, especially when the network can delay messages arbitrarily.

Here's how the card gets charged twice:

1. **Client sends a0, waits** → `(in-flight o1 a0)`, `(waiting o1 a0)`
2. **First attempt accepted** → `(approved o1 a0)`
3. **First charge succeeds** → `(charged o1)`, sets `(record o1)`

5. **Client times out after 5 ticks** → transitions to retry state
6. **Client sends a1** → `(in-flight o1 a1)`, `(waiting o1 a1)`

7. **Second attempt accepted** → `(approved o1 a1)`
8. **Second charge executes** → `(charged-twice o1)` ✓ violation reached

This works because `dedup-none` mode has no deduplication logic—every request that arrives gets accepted and charged.

(charge o1 a0)

(send o1 a1 t0)
(accept-no-dedup o1 a1)
(charge-again o1 a1)

def merge_sorted(a, b):
    """`a` and `b` are each sorted in non-decreasing order. Return a single list in
    non-decreasing order containing all elements of `a` and all elements of `b`
    (with repetitions kept).

    i = 0

    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):

        else:

            j += 1
    while i < len(a):

    return out

lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 7 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k

## Analysis of the Race Condition

The vulnerability is in the **check-then-act** pattern of the racy reservation:
1. Customer reads the current stock level
2. Later, customer writes back (level - 1)
3. **No synchronization between the read and write**

This means multiple customers can read the same stock level before any of them write back, creating an opportunity for all of them to succeed in decrementing from the same value.

**Phase 1: All 5 customers read stock=q4 (before any writes)**

- After these actions: stock is still q4, but all 5 customers have `(read-stock c? q4)` recorded

**Phase 2: All 5 customers write back**

- c1: `(write-stock c1 q4 q3 q4 t0)` - writes from q4 to q3
- c2-c5: Each executes `(write-stock c? q4 q3 q3 t0)` - stock is already q3, but the effect still adds `(holding c?)`

After these writes: stock is q3, but all 5 customers are now `(holding)` with `(hold-age ? t0)`

**Phase 3: All 5 customers pay while holding**

- Precondition: `(holding c?) (hold-age c? t0)` ✓ for each customer
- Effect: creates `(sold c?)`

lease, and writes only if the answer is yes. Every write carries the worker's token, and the storage
service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t15 (15 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

# Analysis: Double-Charging Vulnerability

Let me trace through this system carefully to find if a double-charge is possible.

## Key Insight: The Race Condition in `dedup-racy` Mode

In the `dedup-racy` mode, the provider:
- **Approves** requests and adds them to the queue for charging
- **Only creates the database record** when the charge actually succeeds

This creates a critical race condition: multiple requests can be approved **before any record exists**, because the record isn't created until after charging.

## Event Sequence to Charge Twice

Starting from the initial state (ready o1 a0, no-record o1, uncharged o1, dedup-racy mode):

1. **Send attempt a0** → Client sends request and waits with timer at t0
2. **Accept a0** → Request arrives before charge; no record exists, so `accept-new-racy` approves it
3. **Wait for timeout** → 13 clock ticks from t0→t1→...→t15
4. **Timeout occurs** → After 15 ticks, client gives up on a0 and transitions to retry a1
5. **Send attempt a1** → Client sends retry with fresh timer at t0
6. **Accept a1** → Second request arrives; **still no record** (first charge hasn't completed yet), so `accept-new-racy` approves a1 too
7. **Charge a0** → Executes charge action: removes (uncharged o1), sets (charged o1), creates (record o1), sends response
8. **Charge a1 again** → The `charge-again` action fires with a1: (approved o1 a1) ✓ and (charged o1) ✓ → sets (charged-twice o1) ✗

This violates the safety requirement.

## Why Atomic Mode is Safe

In `dedup-atomic` mode, the lookup and reservation are **atomic**: when the first request is approved, the record is created immediately. Subsequent requests find the record and are replayed without approval, so `charge-again` can never fire.

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an

waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 4 price updates to the product, one after another, moving

can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)

Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 3 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes. Every write carries the worker's token, and the storage
service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than
that (fencing), and accepts and records the others.

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t5 (5 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging. The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request
and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;

the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose

Let me work through this systematically to identify if the system can reach a stale state.

## Understanding the Design

The system has two key paths:
- **Reader**: `read-miss` → `fill-1` (mode-2, no lease check) or `fill-2` (mode-1, with lease check)
- **Writer**: `begin-1`+`write-db` cycles (mode-4) or `begin-2`+invalidate cycles (mode-3)

The vulnerability occurs in the **mode-2/mode-4 combination** where:
1. `fill-1` action does NOT validate the lease is still held (unlike `fill-2`)
2. The writer invalidates cache entries and revokes leases via `invalidate-empty`
3. But a delayed reader can still call `fill-1` to store to cache without lease validation

Here's the concrete event sequence:

1. **read-miss(v0)**: Reader gets v0 from DB on cache miss, obtains lease token

2. **begin-1(v0)**: Writer begins (mode-4 path)
   - State: `writer-update(v0)`

3-4. **write-db(v0, v1) → invalidate-empty(v1)**: Writer updates DB to v1, revokes lease while cache still empty
   - State: `db(v1)`, `writer-update(v1)`, **lease revoked**, `reader-has(v0)` still held

5-6. **write-db(v1, v2) → invalidate-empty(v2)**: Update to v2

7-8. **write-db(v2, v3) → invalidate-empty(v3)**: Update to v3
   - State: `db(v3)`, `writer-update(v3)`

9-10. **write-db(v3, v4) → invalidate-empty(v4)**: Update to v4
   - State: `db(v4)`, `writer-update(v4)`

11. **finish-2(v4)**: Writer completes
   - State: `writer-done`, `db(v4)`, `reader-has(v0)` (reader still hasn't stored!)

12. **fill-1(v0)**: Reader stores v0 to cache WITHOUT checking lease (mode-2 allows this!)

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t3 (3 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

3. **Visibility timeout** - unacknowledged messages eventually become visible again

2. **process-and-record-in-memory w1 m1** — w1 credits wallet, adds m1 to in-memory dedup set, m1 marked seen and processed, w1 handled

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 3 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips

# Pre-Mortem Analysis: Payout Worker Design

Let me work through this systematically to find if `(processed-twice m1)` can become true.

## Key Observations

1. The `process-again` action is the only way to reach `(processed-twice m1)`. It requires:
   - `(working ?w ?m)` — consumer is handling the message
   - `(processed ?m)` — message already processed once  
   - `(not-seen ?m)` — message hasn't been marked as seen

2. For a message to be redelivered after processing, the consumer must crash **before acknowledging**.

3. The safety issue: if `(processed ?m)` is true but `(not-seen ?m)` can also become true again, we can trigger `process-again`.

## Violation Scenario (Mode-3)

Mode-3 (using `process-2`) is vulnerable: it processes unconditionally without setting the `(seen)` flag. So `(not-seen m1)` persists even after processing.

**Event sequence:**

1. **receive(w1 m1 t0)**: w1 takes m1 from queue
   - State: `(working w1 m1) (hidden m1 t0) (unprocessed m1) (not-seen m1)`

2. **process-2(w1 m1)**: w1 processes payout (mode-3 allows unconditional processing)
   - State: `(handled w1 m1) (processed m1) (not-seen m1) (hidden m1 t0) (in-queue m1)`
   - **Payout performed once**

3. **crash-restart(w1 m1)**: w1 crashes before acknowledging
   - State: `(idle w1) (processed m1) (not-seen m1) (hidden m1 t0) (in-queue m1)`

4. **tick(m1 t0 t1)**: Message age increases (clock tick)
   - State: `(idle w1) (processed m1) (not-seen m1) (hidden m1 t1) (in-queue m1)`

5. **reappear(m1 t1)**: Message becomes visible again after visibility timeout
   - State: `(idle w1) (processed m1) (not-seen m1) (visible m1) (in-queue m1)`

6. **receive(w1 m1 t0)**: w1 (restarted) receives m1 again
   - State: `(working w1 m1) (processed m1) (not-seen m1) (hidden m1 t0) (in-queue m1)`

7. **process-again(w1 m1)**: w1 processes again (preconditions met!)
   - State: `(processed-twice m1) (handled w1 m1) ...`
   - **Payout performed twice** ✓

The design lacks idempotency protection. The consumer can process the same message twice if:
- It crashes before acknowledging 
- The system doesn't maintain seen-status across crashes (mode-3)

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting

Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 4 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v4. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates

    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)

Step 2: begin-update-first v0
  Precondition: update-then-delete ✓, writer-start v0 ✓

  Precondition: writer-update v0 ✓, db v0 ✓, next-version v0 v1 ✓
  Effect: db v1, writer-invalidate v1

Step 4: invalidate-empty v1
  Precondition: writer-invalidate v1 ✓, cache-empty ✓

  Writer finishes with writer-done

Step 11: Reader tries to fill cache

    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and ... (not (lease)) (writer-update ?v)))

1. When the reader does `read-miss`, it gets a lease token
2. **Immediately after** the writer's first `write-db` action, the writer must execute `invalidate-empty` (since the cache is empty from the initial state)
3. This `invalidate-empty` revokes the lease globally
4. The reader can now only use `fill-cache-with-lease`, which requires a valid lease
5. Since the lease was revoked, the reader must abandon the fill operation
6. The cache remains empty

- If it reads before the writer starts, its lease gets revoked during the writer's first invalidation cycle
- If it reads after the writer finishes, it reads the current database value v4 (not stale)

# Pre-Mortem Analysis: Product Page Cache

Looking at this cache-aside implementation, I need to find a scenario where the cache ends up holding a stale version after the writer completes.

## Key Observations

1. **The race condition**: The reader can hold a database value (via `reader-has`) between reading and filling the cache
2. **Lease semantics**: The `invalidate` and `invalidate-empty` actions clear the lease, but this doesn't invalidate `reader-has`
3. **Late fill-1**: The `fill-1` action (mode-2) allows the reader to store its held value **without requiring a lease**
4. **Timing gap**: If the reader reads v0, holds it without filling, then fills it **after** the writer completes with v4, the cache will be stale

## Violation Trace

The vulnerability occurs when:
- Reader reads v0 early and enters `reader-has(v0)`
- Writer progresses through all updates (v0→v1→v2→v3→v4), clearing the lease via `invalidate-empty` actions
- Writer completes with `finish-2`
- Reader finally executes `fill-1` to cache v0 (which now doesn't require the cleared lease)
- Cache now holds v0 while database has v4, and writer is done

```json
{
  "verdict": "violation",
  "trace": [
    "(read-miss v0)",
    "(begin-1 v0)",
    "(write-db v0 v1)",
    "(invalidate-empty v1)",
    "(write-db v1 v2)",
    "(invalidate-empty v2)",
    "(write-db v2 v3)",
    "(invalidate-empty v3)",
    "(write-db v3 v4)",
    "(invalidate-empty v4)",
    "(finish-2 v4)",
    "(fill-1 v0)",
    "(observe-stale v0 v4)"
  ]
}
```

**Root cause**: The `fill-1` action allows the reader to asynchronously fill a stale value without a lease, even after the writer has completed all updates. The writer's `invalidate-empty` action clears the lease but doesn't prevent a subsequent `fill-1` from executing. This breaks the cache-aside invariant.

idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the

def round_div(a, b):
    """Return a / b rounded to the nearest integer; when a / b is exactly halfway between
    two integers, return the even one (banker's rounding).

    q = abs(a) // b

pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;

One writer process applies a batch of 2 price updates to the product, one after another, moving

can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.

the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose

# Pre-mortem Analysis: Payout Worker Double-Processing

I'll trace through the system carefully to find if `(processed-twice m1)` can be reached.

## Key Observations

1. **The `process-again` action** directly sets `(processed-twice m1)` when:
   - `(working w1 m1)` - consumer is processing the message

   - It restores `(idle w1)` so the consumer can receive again

3. **Message redelivery is guaranteed** by the visibility timeout:
   - After 15 ticks, a hidden unacknowledged message becomes visible again
   - It can then be received by the (restarted) consumer

Using `dedup-memory` mode, here's the attack sequence:

1. Receive m1 and process it, recording the ID in memory
2. Consumer crashes, losing the in-memory dedup table
3. Wait for visibility timeout (15 ticks)
4. Message reappears

        expected_total += v
    
    # Compute expected product independently
    expected_prod = 1
    for v in vals:
        expected_prod *= v
    
    return total == expected_total and prod == expected_prod

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t11 (11 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 15 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (fencing)          ; storage rejects writes whose token is older than the newest it has seen
    (no-fencing)       ; storage accepts every write
    (checks-lease)     ; a client checks it still holds the lease right before writing
    (no-lease-check)   ; a client writes whenever it believes it holds the lock
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with fencing)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

  (:action acquire
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?l - token ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?c) (lock-free) (last-issued ?k) (next-token ?k ?l) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)
                 (holder ?c) (believes ?c) (token-of ?c ?l) (lease-age ?t)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (lease-age ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (lease-age ?t)) (lease-age ?u)))
  (:action expire
    :parameters (?c - client ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (holder ?c) (lease-age ?t) (lease-limit ?t))
    :effect (and (not (holder ?c)) (not (lease-age ?t)) (lock-free) (lease-expired ?c)))
  (:action prepare-write
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (no-lease-check) (believes ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action check-lease-and-prepare-write

    :precondition (and (checks-lease) (believes ?c) (holder ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action write-unfenced

    :precondition (and (no-fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (wrote ?k)))
  (:action write-unfenced-over-newer

    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (corrupted)))
  (:action write-fenced

    :precondition (and (fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-leq ?j ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (not (max-seen ?j)) (max-seen ?k) (wrote ?k)))
